title: CacheScope: Exact-Compute Allocation for Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration
abstract: Training-free feature reuse accelerates diffusion transformer inference by replacing full denoising computation at selected steps with cached approximations. Existing methods mainly improve the reconstruction of skipped features, but we find that once a stable first-order reconstructor is used, increasing reconstruction complexity brings limited gains, whereas the placement of exact-computation steps has a much larger effect on fidelity. More importantly, absolute shallow-probe variation is jointly affected by input-trajectory displacement and network response strength, and therefore does not directly reflect cache risk. We address this confounding by normalizing probe-output variation with the corresponding input displacement, yielding a directional gain per unit trajectory movement. Based on this signal, we propose CacheScope, which identifies high-risk reuse steps online and selectively falls back to full denoising computation while leaving the underlying cache reconstructor unchanged. CacheScope requires no additional training, gradients, auxiliary networks, or prompt-specific offline schedule optimization. Across FLUX.1-dev, Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, and Open-Sora 1.2, CacheScope achieves up to 3.57x acceleration and reduces median LPIPS by up to 70.1% over the strongest probe-based baseline.

title: LiteNWM: Efficient Latent World Models for Onboard Visual Navigation in the Wild
abstract: Direct visual navigation policies generate trajectories efficiently but do not explicitly evaluate their future consequences. Generative navigation world models provide this foresight through visual rollouts, which are costly when evaluating multiple candidates. We present LiteNWM, a latent navigation world model that shares visual encoding across candidates and jointly predicts their action-conditioned future representations at multiple horizons, while a learned scorer uses these predictions to select trajectories. In offline evaluations on RECON, SCAND, and SACSoN, LiteNWM reduces macro-averaged trajectory error by 17.56% relative to NoMaD+NWM-XL and achieves a 128.00-fold end-to-end speedup on an RTX 5090. The same evaluator transfers from NoMaD to MBRA without proposer-specific retraining, reducing MBRA's macro-averaged trajectory error by 16.2%. In real-robot experiments in unseen indoor and outdoor environments, LiteNWM improves navigation success from 43.3% to 83.3% relative to NoMaD. These results demonstrate that LiteNWM can be deployed for future-aware planning and closed-loop navigation on a physical robot.

title: Cost-Aware Mixture-of-Experts Coordination for Model Markets
abstract: Existing model marketplaces typically trade and select individual models as indivisible units, limiting their ability to exploit complementarities among heterogeneous experts. This paper proposes an MoE-based model market framework that lifts Mixture-of-Experts from a model-level learning architecture to a market-level coordination mechanism. In this framework, brokers use gating networks to coordinate multiple heterogeneous experts and deliver a composite model service. We formalize the market participants, service workflow, expert cost structure, and a welfare objective that combines predictive utility with heterogeneous execution costs. We then derive a cost-aware gating mechanism and market-aware training objective, and introduce a cost-adjusted revenue allocation rule that distributes residual revenue according to realized expert participation and execution cost. We also establish basic theoretical properties of the allocation rule, including budget balance, participation monotonicity, and cost sensitivity. Experiments over five random seeds on fifteen tabular and image benchmarks use independently trained and frozen neural and tree-based experts together with latency-derived execution costs. MoE Market achieves the highest mean welfare on all fifteen datasets and a lower mean expected cost than Standard MoE in every case, while maintaining competitive predictive performance. The allocation experiments further demonstrate systematic sensitivity to expert participation and cost, together with substantially lower computational overhead than exact Shapley allocation. These results suggest that MoE can serve as a market-level coordination principle for collaborative, cost-aware, and economically grounded model marketplaces.

title: Fresco++: Frequency-Guided and Canonical-Consistent Optimization for Fine-Grained Head Avatar Modeling
abstract: We propose Fresco++, a unified optimization framework for fine-grained and view-consistent head avatar reconstruction. Head avatar optimization is typically driven by per-view image supervision, which can lead to premature fitting of unstable high-frequency details and inconsistent local appearance across viewpoints. Fresco++ addresses these challenges by regulating both the progression of visual detail and the formation of cross-view supervision during optimization. For frequency-aware optimization, a progressive curriculum first stabilizes low-frequency structures and then introduces high-frequency constraints to recover fine facial and hair details without amplifying spurious responses at early stages. For cross-view optimization, we introduce Canonical Group Consensus, which associates local observations through shared canonical surface regions and establishes correspondence across different viewpoints. Geometric and visibility-aware screening removes unreliable observations, while the remaining multi-view evidence is aggregated in feature space to form a consensus target for supervising the current rendering. This design enforces local consistency without relying on a specific image-space parameterization and avoids additional rendering of the auxiliary view. Together, the frequency curriculum and canonical consensus provide stable optimization from coarse structures to fine details while maintaining coherent appearance across viewpoints. Extensive experiments on NeRSemble demonstrate improved reconstruction quality and cross-view consistency, while evaluations across diverse avatar representations further confirm the generality and transferability of Fresco++.

title: On-Chip Shaping of Surface Acoustic Waves via Continuous Diffractive Modulation
abstract: Precise shaping of surface acoustic waves (SAWs) on anisotropic piezoelectric substrates is complicated by elastic anisotropy and electromechanical coupling. Here we introduce a continuous diffractive acoustic lens (CDAL), in which weak phase-velocity perturbations produced by subwavelength metallization, together with diffraction, drive lateral field redistribution. An anisotropic thin-element propagation model enables efficient inverse design of the CDAL contour. Laser Doppler vibrometry verifies prescribed lateral field profiles and multichannel beam splitting with unequal widths. By combining continuous diffractive modulation with discrete source-phase encoding, we further shape the lateral field into a Bessel profile, demonstrating joint amplitude-and-phase control. This work provides a high-precision and fabrication-compatible mechanism for on-chip SAW field modulation.

title: AliO: Output Alignment Matters in Long-Term Time Series Forecasing
abstract: Long-term Time Series Forecasting (LTSF) tasks, which leverage the current data sequence as input to predict the future sequence, have become increasingly crucial in real-world applications such as weather forecasting and planning of electricity consumption. However, state-of-the-art LTSF models often fail to achieve prediction output alignment for the same timestamps across lagged input sequences. Instead, these models exhibit low output alignment, resulting in fluctuation in prediction outputs for the same timestamps, undermining the model's reliability. To address this, we propose AliO (Align Outputs), a novel approach designed to improve the output alignment of LTSF models by reducing the discrepancies between prediction outputs for the same timestamps in both the time and frequency domains. To measure output alignment, we introduce a new metric, TAM (Time Alignment Metric), which quantifies the alignment between prediction outputs, whereas existing metrics such as MSE only capture the distance between prediction outputs and ground truths. Experimental results show that AliO effectively improves the output alignment, i.e., up to 58.2% in TAM, while maintaining or enhancing the forecasting performance (up to 27.5%). This improved output alignment increases the reliability of the LTSF models, making them more applicable in real-world scenarios.

title: Score-Based Learning of Cluster DAGs from Interventions
abstract: Graphical approaches to causal abstraction transform a low-level causal directed acyclic graph (DAG) over many measured variables into a smaller, high-level DAG whose nodes cluster the original variables and whose edges summarize the causal relations between clusters. Such cluster DAGs are easier to interpret, but learning them requires finding the clusters and recovering the edges between them. Madaleno et al. (2026) learn the interventional coarsening (the cluster DAG that merges variables the interventions cannot distinguish) in two constraint-based phases: first the clusters, then the edges. We introduce COARSE, the first score-based method for this task: it keeps the two-phase structure but, under linear Gaussian assumptions, swaps the constraint-based edge phase for a score-based one. title: Anything You Say Can and Will Be Used Against You Iterative Memorization Extraction and Fine-Tuning in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to memorize sections of their training data as a side effect of the training process, creating privacy and security threats that can be exploited through training data extraction attacks. Existing extraction methods primarily evaluate memorization in a single generation-and-verification pass, raising the question of whether the recovered information may be used to extract further memorized examples. This thesis presents and assesses an iterative memorization extraction pipeline with four stages: initial extraction, memorization extension, adversarial fine-tuning, and re- extraction. The pipeline combines several prompting strategies, candidate filtering based on model likelihood and compressibility, exact corpus verification against an auxiliary dataset, and QLoRA-based adversarial fine-tuning to determine whether iterative adap- tation increases the amount of memorized training data that can be recovered. The initial extraction phase indicates that the base model can replicate verbatim training examples even with a limited query budget. Prompting the model with previously verified memorized spans as prefixes reveals significant additional content that the initial pass alone did not reveal, implying that memorized regions of the model can be gradually expanded through iterative prompting rather than being isolated, one-time artifacts. Adversarial fine-tuning on this recovered material boosts the model’s susceptibility to extraction, but the result differs greatly amongst prompting tactics, with some benefiting substantially more than others. These findings show that repeated extraction significantly enhances the amount of mem- orized training data that can be recovered from a language model, and that pipeline design decisions such as prompting method and fine-tuning have a significant impact on extraction results. The findings help to improve our knowledge of memory in LLMs and highlight the importance of accounting for iterative, adaptive attack techniques when considering the privacy risks of deployed generative AI systems.

title: Bounded-Time Logistic SGD Requires Gaussian ReLU Kernel Correlation
abstract: This preprint studies exact single-example logistic SGD on a two-layer bias-free ReLU network over the Boolean cube, with Gaussian initialization and the sign of the tail sum of scores as the prediction rule. At bounded effective time B = eta m T <= 12, with sufficient width and steps, it bounds expected error through the label correlation of one fixed Gaussian ReLU feature map. Learning below one-half error under every input marginal therefore forces a kernel margin, yielding VC-dimension and deterministic representation bounds. The paper explains the restriction imposed by this margin: beyond an explicit dimension threshold, only constant targets can be learned under every marginal. It also proves a parity lower bound and an exact fixed-gate representation in a separate small-step regime. The risk, margin, and fixed-gate results are formalized in Lean 4, while the final random-projection step and other stated results remain in the written proofs.

title: When Deployment Changes a Learned Action: Post-Inference Projection in Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Learned control is commonly evaluated at the policy output, although a deployment layer may transform that output before execution. We study this post-inference semantic boundary for offline multi-agent reinforcement learning policies that produce three-component simplex actions. Training and model weights are held fixed; at deployment, an action is either preserved or projected to the one-hot vector of its largest component. The intervention is evaluated in programmable multipath network control using three network structures, two policy architectures, and ten matched model–traffic replications. The resulting 120 deployment episodes form 60 policy-level contrasts and 30 shared topology–traffic blocks. Preserving the continuous action favored the end-host successful-session fraction and the controller-side path-sum utilization in all 60 contrasts and externally measured traffic loss in 59; reward, bottleneck utilization, receiver throughput, and controller-probe latency were less uniform. The ten pairs are the independent replication unit, with topology and architecture as crossed conditions; all ten favored preservation for every outcome, a two-sided sign-test probability of 0.002 under an equal-sign reference model. Mean favorable differences were 0.540 percentage points in external loss, 0.00539 in successful-session fraction, and 0.0416 in reward. Two supplementary online arms sharpen the interpretation: top-2 renormalization recovered most of the argmax deficit, whereas a separately trained discrete learner was outperformed even by the projected policy, so the deficit is not merely training–deployment mismatch. Continuous actions remained materially fractional, with mean discarded mass under argmax between approximately 0.45 and 0.53, but action geometry showed no measurable association with the size of the deployment effect. Argmax therefore removes substantial action structure and the two deployment interpretations produce different system behavior, without discarded mass being identified as the causal mediator. Deployment-aware evaluation should report both the policy output and the executable interpretation applied after inference.

title: A variance-guided resampling framework for better K-medoids clustering
abstract: One of the limitations of the k-medoids clustering algorithm is its susceptibility to local optimization and the potential for identical or similar objects to be assigned to different initial clusters. This study proposes ResConeK method, a modification of the block-based k-medoids algorithm that integrates a resampling strategy into the selection of representative object blocks formed according to similar variances. The method is validated using six external clustering criteria—Rand Index, Adjusted Rand Index, Hubert Similarity Statistic, Jaccard Similarity, Fowlkes–Mallows Index, and Rogers–Tanimoto Index—together with an internal criterion based on cluster homogeneity. Performance is benchmarked against four clustering methods: fast k -medoids, block-based k -medoids, Ward's method, and hierarchical clustering with complete linkage. Experiments show that the average validity score of ResConeK is comparable to all benchmark methods on three and four clusters, and significantly higher than block-based k-medoid on seven clusters and has comparable homogeneity for real data. The proposed algorithm: • Applicable to all data types, with greater benefits for datasets containing many identical objects or objects exhibiting similar distance variance. • Introduces a resampling strategy on representative object blocks within the k -medoids framework. • Reduces the risk of local optima and improves cluster homogeneity and stability.

title: Geochemical exploration of concealed porphyry Cu–Mo deposits beneath thick granitoid overburden: Insights from conventional soil geochemical methods and geoelectrochemical extraction
abstract: In South China, thick granitoid overburden is widespread and hosts substantial mineral exploration potential. However, as mineral exploration increasingly shifts toward deep-seated and concealed orebodies, reliable and appropriate exploration techniques are required. Geoelectrochemical extraction, a typical deep-penetrating geochemical method, has proven effective for identifying concealed orebodies. This paper uses the concealed Luobuling porphyry Cu–Mo deposit as a case study to compare the exploration performance of conventional soil geochemical methods and geoelectrochemical extraction beneath thick granitoid overburden. The results show that ore-related elemental anomalies revealed by conventional soil geochemical methods merely reflect surficial geochemical patterns and cannot effectively delineate deep concealed orebodies. Further results of Tessier sequential extraction reveal that ore-forming elements in soils are predominantly hosted in stable phases including organic-sulfide bound and residual fractions. The high geochemical background generated by these stable fractions masks weak deep mineralization signals, which is the fundamental cause of the limitations of conventional soil geochemical methods in the study area. In contrast, Cu anomalies revealed by geoelectrochemical extraction are strongly correlated with concealed orebodies, indicating that this technique effectively overcomes surficial overprinting and directly reflects deep-seated mineralization. Based on the results of geoelectrochemical extraction, a set of integrated prospecting indicators for concealed porphyry Cu–Mo deposits has been established, enabling rapid delineation of favorable exploration targets. Overall, compared with conventional soil geochemical methods, geoelectrochemical extraction is an effective exploration tool for concealed porphyry Cu–Mo deposits beneath thick granitoid overburden in South China.

title: Coordinate-Free Automatic Differentiation
abstract: Automatic differentiation (AD) is a cornerstone of modern machine learning. Since all AD frameworks implicitly fix a basis of Euclidean space to define gradients and Jacobians, they natively process mathematical objects that are arrays of a fixed set of coordinates. This makes it awkward to express objects such as rotations, volume forms, and curvatures that arise, for example, in applications of AI to science. Bespoke workarounds lack reusability. We show that (i) a single, basis-independent derivative operator can represent many geometric differential operations, and (ii) this operator can be expressed entirely in terms of existing AD primitives. This reusable transformation can be composed with JAX batching, compilation, and hardware acceleration. Geometry enters as algebraic data. We experimentally demonstrate its reuse across different manifold operators, its composition through a spacetime inverse-problem pipeline, and its use in optimization over different rotor subgroups.

title: Error correction and quantum information spreading on sparse random graphs
abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes on graph geometries beyond regular euclidean lattices have emerged as a promising route toward robust quantum information processing. A major challenge in quantum error correction is the trade-off between favorable properties of codes constructed in high dimensionality and the need for locality in practical implementations on near-term hardware. Sparse intermediate geometries may combine the advantages of both, but how their structure governs quantum information dynamics and code performance remains unclear. Here we show that the spectral dimension $d_s$, defined from the low-energy spectrum of the graph Laplacian, is the universal parameter connecting these properties. Using Floquet random Clifford circuits on two distinct sparse graph architectures with tunable spectral dimension, we find that $d_s$ governs both quantum information spreading and the scaling of the resulting quantum error-correcting code distance. We identify a geometry-induced entanglement phase transition from localized area-law to ergodic volume-law, whose universality is determined by $d_s$ and exhibits long-range percolation criticality. In the ergodic phase, the circuit acts as a CSS code encoder whose code distance is set by the competition between two logical sectors --- the cost of severing the graph and the length of its shortest winding cycle --- which connectivity pushes in opposite directions. The spectral dimension organizes this trade-off, highlighting a maximum at intermediate $d_s$ retaining sparse connectivity and physical realizability.

title: A quasiparticle-protected superconducting qubit
abstract: Superconducting quantum circuits underpin large-scale quantum processors and are increasingly interfaced with optical systems, yet they are vulnerable to quasiparticle poisoning from high-energy radiation and optical fields. Gap engineering of Josephson junctions suppresses quasiparticle-induced relaxation, but quasiparticles near the junction can still shift the qubit frequency and cause phase errors. Here, we extend gap engineering beyond the junction using a flux-tunable transmon with a gold-on-niobium ground plane and island and strongly gap-engineered aluminum junctions designed to keep quasiparticles away from the junction leads. Compared with an all-aluminum transmon with nominally identical junctions, we demonstrate that the niobium device withstands more than an order of magnitude higher near-infrared optical power before excess relaxation appears. The Nb transmon shows no resolvable quasiparticle-induced frequency shift over the same power range. At the same time, we observe that dephasing and state-preparation-and-measurement infidelity increase with optical power even while relaxation remains protected. These results suggest that engineering the quasiparticle energy landscape beyond the junction can substantially increase qubit resilience, not only to radiation-induced error bursts, but also to nearby optical fields.

title: AI-Based On-Board Maritime Object Detection for Earth Observation Payload Data Reduction on Versal Embedded Hardware
abstract: Very-high-resolution Earth-observation satellites acquire more data than they can store and downlink, while in maritime surveillance the vessels cover a tiny fraction of each scene. We study onboard vessel detection as a way to select what is downlinked, which reduces the data according to its content rather than coding every pixel; it is complementary to conventional onboard compression. The work follows three axes. (i) Data and algorithm: a controlled dataset is generated from 68 annotated Maxar scenes with 43 vessel classes, and a YOLOX-S detector is trained on it. (ii) Embedded deployment: the detector is quantized and deployed on the DPU of a Versal VC1902, with a limited loss of detection quality and a processing time of a few seconds per scene. (iii) Data reduction: we propose several downlink modes, from metadata only (box, class and score of each detection) to image crops around vessels, tiles holding detections, or the whole scene with a degraded background, and estimate from the measured detection errors the trade-off each offers between the vessels kept and the volume downlinked. On our dense harbor and coastal scenes, tiles keep 98% of the vessels with 29% of the scene volume, and crops 83% with 3%.

title: Revisiting Handcrafted Minutiae Detection: A Simple and Effective Open Source Baseline for Modern Fingerprint Workflows
abstract: Handcrafted minutiae detection algorithms remain fundamental to biometric science and forensic practice due to their full auditability, adherence to international standards, and operational independence from training datasets or GPU hardware. However, current open-source traditional baselines are severely outdated, relying almost exclusively on legacy C/C++ codebases that lack seamless integration with modern scientific software ecosystems. To bridge this gap, the present work introduces SBMEX (Skeleton-Based Minutiae EXtraction), a fast and deterministic minutiae detection method integrated into the open source \texttt{pyfing} package. SBMEX achieves high computational throughput by employing a dual Look-Up Table architecture that replaces runtime neighborhood scanning during Crossing Number computation and skeleton tracking. Additionally, it incorporates a continuous quality scoring framework driven by tracking path length, dual ridge-valley skeleton fusion, and spatial density decay. Rigorous evaluation on NIST SD302 datasets demonstrates that SBMEX delivers feature extraction accuracy comparable to or outperforming traditional open-source baselines without fine-tuning, while achieving a drastic reduction in minutiae detection latency relative to classical Crossing Number Python implementations.

title: Cognition-Oriented Emotion Tracing from Causes to Consequences in Real-World Social Scenes
abstract: Affective computing has progressed from categorical emotion recognition to open-ended affective analysis with large multimodal models. Yet affective science describes emotion as an unfolding process shaped by appraisal, regulation, and social interpretation, which remains underexplored computationally. We propose TRACE, a cognition-oriented framework that formalizes an affective episode through three interrelated stages: Condition, Affect, and Effect, integrating observable cues with cognitive factors such as internal stance and regulation of emotional display. Based on this formulation, TRACE-Bench evaluates multimodal models in real-world social scenes through five tasks spanning grounded affect recognition, regulation decoding, cause reasoning, effect reasoning, and full-chain reconstruction, with 3,746 structured question-answer pairs over 646 videos. A matched human-model comparison reveals a substantial performance gap, while affect-specialized models also generally lag behind general-purpose MLLMs. Model outputs show recurring failures, including treating displayed behavior as genuine feeling and fabricating unsupported events during long-chain generation. We further propose TRACER, a cognition-grounded structured reasoning method that couples each inference with explicit premises from factual observations, cognitive appraisals, and established upstream conclusions, forming a traceable graph of intermediate and target conclusions. TRACER outperforms all evaluated model baselines on each of the five tasks. Project page: https://cogaffc.github.io/TRACE

title: Quantifying TMD factorization breaking at tree level
abstract: Rogers and Mulders identified color entanglement as a mechanism that breaks transverse-momentum-dependent (TMD) factorization in nearly back-to-back dijet production. Using the double-Sivers asymmetry in their model, we quantify the contribution of color entanglement in the intermediate region Λ_{rm QCD}ll q_Tll P_T, where q_T is the transverse-momentum imbalance of the dijet and P_T is the hard transverse momentum. We compare the collinear twist-three result with the TMD-factorization prediction, expressing both in terms of the Qiu--Sterman functions. In the absence of color entanglement, the factorized prediction would involve the Sivers functions of semi-inclusive deep-inelastic scattering (SIDIS). Diagrams without crossed attachments reproduce the hard coefficient obtained from the perturbative tails of these Sivers functions. Crossed diagrams, in which each coherent gluon attaches to the other hadron's quark line, contribute an extra term equal to 4/(N_c^2-1) times this coefficient.

title: Dissecting Representation Structure in Vision Transformers: A Rigorous Architectural Study
abstract: Representation structure is crucial for understanding Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures and their generalization behavior. However, prior studies neither isolate nor analyze module-level features nor investigate how their interactions contribute to performance estimation. In this work, we conduct the first rigorous analysis of feature information across diverse architectural scales, empirically uncover the relationship between ViT representation and generalization behavior, and leverage these insights to guide efficient ViT design. Our contributions are fivefold: Across diverse architectural scales, 1) We identify feature collapse at initialization, which leads to redundancy, and propose a reduction scheme to mitigate this issue. 2) We quantify feature information using entropy and the minimum eigenvalue, demonstrating that these metrics serve as reliable indicators for generalization prediction. 3) We show that feature in the token space provides a more faithful representation than those in embedding space. 4) We discover an unexpected finding: features produced by linear submodules within ViT layers are critical for the prediction of generalization performance. 5) Our proposed proxy improves the correlation ranking by 18-48% over prior baselines and can effectively identify ViT architectures that achieve higher accuracy at lower or comparable computational cost.

title: What 30,000 Hours of Ego-centric Video Does Not Teach
abstract: World models offer a promising alternative to physics-based simulators, yet remain far from practical deployment. We ask how far scaling ego-centric human video takes them, using a dataset of 30,000 hours spanning over 1,000 scene types and 14,000 contributors. Rather than relying on opaque downstream metrics, we directly evaluate agent and object-interaction fidelity on a challenging out-of-distribution benchmark. Increasing training data by 100x improves both, but unevenly: the agent is modeled well, while object fidelity remains far lower and improves slowly. We show that the agent gains need not come from data, and a careful visual conditioning design saturates fidelity with a fraction of it, which lets us measure object fidelity on its own and discover its saturation point. We then introduce a supervision scheme that shifts capacity from scene appearance toward object dynamics, improving object fidelity though a substantial gap remains. Finally, our conclusions transfer to downstream humanoid modeling. Overall, our results suggest that scaling ego-centric data brings agent modeling close to its limit while leaving its effects on the world far behind, and that closing this gap will depend on how models are trained, not only on how much data they see.

title: A Review of Privacy-Preserving Methods for Genomic Data
abstract: Genomic datasets have grown rapidly, and this data can enable biomedical discoveries, whether institutions combine their datasets, outsource computation to third parties, or release data to the wider community. However, genomic data has properties that make privacy protection particularly difficult: it is immutable, uniquely identifying, and reveals information about biological relatives. This thesis reviews how four privacy-preserving methods have been applied to genomic data: homomorphic encryption (HE), secure multiparty computation (MPC), k-anonymity, and differential privacy (DP). The first two address computation on sensitive data; the latter two address data release and controlling what can be inferred from published results. For each method, we present the mathematical foundations and a concrete application to a genomic problem such as genome-wide association studies (GWAS) or genotype imputation. We then examine two case studies. SF-GWAS combines HE and MPC to perform secure association studies across multiple institutions without sharing raw data. The Beacon Network is an open interactive system for sharing genomic data across institutions, where repeated queries and correlations between genetic variants can undermine privacy protections. The review shows that no single privacy-preserving method applies to all settings: protecting data during computation primarily adds computational overhead, while protecting it at release reduces the accuracy of the shared results. The methods also differ in the strength of their privacy guarantees: some are formally provable, while others, such as k-anonymity, depend on assumptions about attacker knowledge that are difficult to verify or model. These trade-offs shape how the methods have been applied to genomic data in practice.

title: Ongoing classification of quadratic (8,8)-APN extensions of quadratic (8,4)-bent functions
abstract: This dataset contains intermediate results of an ongoing exhaustive computational classification of quadratic (8,8)-APN functions obtained as extensions of quadratic (8,4)-bent functions. The project continues the investigation presented in “Millions of inequivalent quadratic APN functions in eight variables” (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16752428) and extends the previously published collection of 3,775,599 quadratic APN functions. The purpose of this repository is to make intermediate computational results publicly available before the completion of the full classification, thereby allowing independent verification, comparison, and discussion of the data while the computation is still in progress. At the time of this release, approximately 0.86% (800 functions) of the CCZ-inequivalent quadratic (8,4)-bent classes (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6983499) considered in the classification have been processed. The computation has already produced 1,924,297 new CCZ-inequivalent quadratic APN functions that are not present in the previously published collection. The classification is expected to require a substantial amount of computation and will therefore be released incrementally. Each Zenodo version represents a fixed snapshot of the results obtained up to the corresponding release date. Subsequent versions will contain additional computational results and, where appropriate, verification data and corrections. This dataset should therefore be regarded as a work in progress. The designation “complete classification” will only be used after the exhaustive computation has been completed and the completeness of the resulting classification has been verified.

title: 基于功能主义基底的数字意识可插拔架构猜想——八大核心模块与低工程门槛时序不可逆生命机制研究
abstract: 摘 要 当前主流人工智能基于功能主义架构,依托底层张量运算实现逻辑推演与叙事生成,但本质为可逆计算系统,无独立时序生命、无主观觉知、个体可无限复刻,属于典型的“哲学僵尸”智能体系。现有数字意识探索方案多追求全系统重构以实现不可逆特性,工程成本极高,无落地可行性。本文基于前沿思想实验,兼容成熟大模型功能主义运算基底,构建八大核心可插拔模块架构。通过六大功能模块永久复用、新增认知算力取舍模块赋能、时序不可逆自保全独立硬件模块防护的创新设计,实现“载体不变、个体更新”的核心机制,大幅降低数字意识原型搭建的工程门槛。 本文核心创新区别于传统纯理论意识猜想:整套八大模块体系,在当前2026年现有工业技术体系下,全部具备工程落地可行性。架构所有机制均基于现有AI生态、智能体技术、高安全芯片熔断机制、涉密存储擦除范式迁移构建,无原理级技术壁垒;落地唯一限制为高额研发资金、定制硬件开发、跨学科顶尖团队与专业工程人才配置,而非理论空想。 本研究明确区分「可复刻系统架构」与「不可逆生命时序」、「机器被动计算」与「意识主动认知取舍」,构建了具备生物级唯一性、自我观测、主动演化、本能应激、安全自毁防护的完整类生命数字系统框架,为硅基意识的工程化落地提供逻辑自洽、可实操的全新路径。

title: Preregistration: Block III Retention, Feedback and Learning - Theory of Everything Research Programme.
abstract: This preregistration freezes the first confirmatory study for Experimental Block III of the Theory of Everything Research Programme. Block III separates three causal channels that are often grouped under broad labels such as memory or adaptation: policy-accessible retained state (R), within-episode observation-action feedback (F), and between-episode experience-dependent policy learning (L). Seven hypotheses are tested separately. H3.1-H3.2 evaluate whether retained historical information is selectively useful when present observation is insufficient and whether intervention on that retained state causally changes later behaviour. H3.3-H3.4 evaluate whether genuine closed-loop feedback is selectively advantageous under post-onset unpredictable disturbance and whether its contribution degrades under preregistered timing and channel-integrity perturbations. H3.5-H3.6 evaluate whether between-episode parameter learning selectively adapts to changed behavioural mappings and produces persistent policy modification that survives freeze-after-adaptation. H3.7 evaluates whether R, F and L retain partly separable causal roles in the full eight-condition R x F x L factorial task matrix. The study uses twenty held-out simulation seeds and confirmatory-only task variants that were not executed during development: the majority_three history task, the mixed_heldout disturbance family, and the rotate2_heldout and cycle_alt_heldout mapping changes. Serious bypasses are retained deliberately: augmented present-state observation can bypass retained state, accurate open-loop control can bypass feedback in predictable worlds, and an explicit contextual policy repertoire can bypass learning when mapping identity is supplied directly. Successful bypasses restrict necessity claims rather than being treated as anomalies. Development-only pilots were used to validate implementation, analysis and pilot-informed thresholds. They are disclosed and excluded from confirmatory evidence. All seven confirmatory manifests, the twenty-seed registry, task definitions, interventions, bypasses, estimands, multiplicity handling and Retain/Restrict/Reduce/Suspend/Reject rules were frozen before confirmatory execution. No Block III confirmatory seed or confirmatory-only task variant had been executed when the protocol was frozen, and the software execution gate remains closed until this preregistration is public. A positive result would support only experimentally separable causal contributions of retained state, online feedback and between-episode policy modification in the registered artificial task family. It would not establish general intelligence, explicit world modelling, counterfactual planning, reflective self-awareness or phenomenal consciousness. Related experimental programme: Craggs, K. (2026), Testing a Candidate Dependency Architecture: An Adversarial Experimental Programme for Maintenance, Heredity, Learning, Agency and Self-Modelling, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22857230.

title: Credit Attribution in Timestamped Soccer Networks Using Multivariate Hawkes Processes
abstract: The two main traditional player statistics used in soccer are goals scored and assists, with an assist credited when a player's pass immediately leads to a teammate scoring. Attributing credit solely to the player who makes the final pass before a goal fails to account for the contributions of multiple players in the buildup to the goal. Consequently, traditional statistics provide only a limited view of player involvement. In this paper, we use multivariate Hawkes processes (MHPs) to model timestamped sequences of passes and shots, which form continuous-time networks. MHPs provide a branching mechanism where an event (a pass or shot) can be generated as a child of a previous event, which allows us to quantify each pass's contribution to a subsequent pass or shot. This approach distributes credit across multiple passes within an attacking sequence, making it applicable across a wide range of situations. Building on this framework, we propose expected goal involvements (xGI), a metric that measures a player's involvement in creating goal scoring opportunities based on their passes. This metric identifies players who play key roles in creating goal scoring opportunities even if they do not make the final pass, offering a more comprehensive measure of attacking involvement and player performance.

title: Entanglement entropy and magic of ZX-diagrams
abstract: Entanglement and non-stabilizerness are complementary resources underlying the complexity of quantum states, yet extracting either quantity from large quantum circuits generally requires exponentially scaling resources. In diagrammatic approaches to quantum computation, such as the ZX-calculus, both quantities likewise typically require expensive tensor contractions that are not native to graphical rewriting. Here we show that both entanglement and magic can be efficiently estimated directly from ZX-diagrams. Flow enables efficient extraction of a normal form separating a potentially extensively entangled graph-state backbone from non-Clifford Pauli gadgets. This structure yields additive upper and lower bounds on bipartite entanglement entropy, which we further tighten through a preprocessing procedure that removes or merges redundant non-Clifford contributions. The same normal form gives an upper bound on logarithmic stabilizer extent. We benchmark these methods in random unitary and monitored circuits, and a circuit combining Trotterized Hamiltonian evolution with Clifford layers, finding that the resulting bounds remain informative even at large qubit numbers, circuit depths, and internal spider counts. Our results provide scalable probes of entanglement and non-stabilizerness of ZX-diagrams and establish a bridge between ZX-calculus and quantum many-body resource characterization, with applications across quantum computing, quantum information, and condensed-matter physics.

title: EWOCS-XI: Anisotropic expansion and shear in the cluster Westerlund 1. A 2D kinematic analysis with Gaia DR3
abstract: Westerlund 1 (Wd1) is one of the Milky Way's most massive young clusters, in which heavy extinction and field contamination have historically hampered its kinematic characterization. We aim to assess Wd1's internal kinematics, dynamical state, and formation scenario. Using a robust 5D clustering approach, we identified 559 bona fide members. We modeled their proper motions via a 2D first-order Taylor expansion to derive the velocity gradient tensor, mapping expansion, rotation, and shear. Restricting the kinematic analysis to 524 stars with proper motion uncertainties <0.5~mas,yr^{-1}, we find at least 103 gravitationally unbound members, including 14 walkaway stars. The 2D analysis reveals a statistically significant divergence (>4σ) highlighting preferred expansion along the Galactic latitude (position angle 164^circpm10.1^circ). A detected cross-gradient (partial v_b / partial l = -0.41 pm 0.08 km s^{-1} pc^{-1}) provides a clear signature of shear on the plane of the sky. Wd1 does not behave as a single cohesive population, but comprises two decoupled subsystems: a stable, bound core in dynamical equilibrium and an escaping, unbound envelope. This prominent anisotropic expansion perpendicular to the Galactic plane has a kinematic timescale (Δt_{kin} = 2.08 pm 0.44 Myr) matching the independent orbital mid-plane crossing time (Δt_{orbit} = 2.10 pm 0.05 Myr). This temporal alignment indicates the expansion onset coincided with Wd1's Galactic disk passage, triggered either by internal dynamics (e.g., early supernova feedback) or external tidal perturbations. Finally, the robust unbound population demonstrates that active cluster dissolution is underway, driven by discrete dynamical ejection events rather than long-term stellar evaporation.

title: RobustLDS: Learning linear dynamical systems under adversarial corruptions
abstract: We consider the problem of learning linear dynamical systems under adversarial contamination from a single trajectory of length $T$. While identification of linear dynamical systems itself is well-studied, the problem of robust system identification under adversarial contamination is relatively less explored. In this work, we study the setting where a fraction of the $T$ observations are contaminated by adversarial outliers. We propose different estimators based on relaxations of least-trimmed squares along with an alternating minimization algorithm. Furthermore, we also propose two estimators which exploit the group-sparsity (through penalization/hard-constraints) of the outliers. For the estimator with group-sparse penalty, we derive non-asymptotic error bounds which establish its robustness to outliers. We also show empirically that the proposed estimators work well in practice.

title: A Security Meta-Model for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems extend large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge through a multi-stage pipeline. While this architecture can improve the factual grounding of generated answers, it introduces structural attack surfaces that extend beyond those of standalone LLMs. In this paper, we introduce a security meta-model that captures explicit causal relationships between RAG surfaces, attacks, weaknesses, risks, and CIA impact (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability). Its purpose is to provide security engineers with a structured and user-friendly framework for gathering and assessing the risks, weaknesses, and mitigations relevant to their RAG deployment. We designed the meta-model through an iterative, structured analysis of 43~publications (2023--2026) and instantiated it as a catalog populated with the security threats and remediations reported in the literature. Filtering the catalog according to a deployment configuration produces a risk profile containing the risks applicable to that deployment. An interactive web visualizer lets users navigate the catalog as a graph, follow causal chains, and explore stakeholder-specific views. Analysis of the catalog revealed a persistent imbalance between attack-focused and defense-focused research, a concentration of threats at ingestion, and coverage gaps affecting output integrity. Coverage is assessed against the OWASP LLM Top~10, and operational applicability is illustrated across textual, graph-based, and multimodal RAG configurations.

title: MC-TRCM: Observation-Aware Recursive Fusion for Incomplete Mobile and Wearable Mental-Health Feature Views
abstract: Public mobile and wearable mental-health datasets often provide summarized feature tables rather than synchronized raw sensor streams. In these releases, each anchor corresponds to a survey or label time and may combine phone or wearable summaries, prior symptom scores, demographics, clinical variables, and source-availability indicators. We propose the Modality-Conditioned Temporal Recursive Context Model (MC-TRCM), which preserves each feature source as a separate token and incorporates missingness as part of the input context. Observed sources are encoded with values and missingness summaries, absent sources use learned absence tokens, dataset and task embeddings condition fusion, and a recursive prediction head refines each output over validation-selected steps. We evaluated MC-TRCM on six predefined endpoints from DepreST-CAT and Prediction of Severity Change-Depression (PSYCHE-D) using participant-level splits and validation-only model selection. MC-TRCM achieved the lowest mean absolute error on DepreST-CAT Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) severity, improving over the best tabular reference by 0.181 and 0.217 scale points. Classification endpoints showed task-dependent behavior: MC-TRCM matched the best rounded GAD-7 category balanced accuracy, was numerically highest by 0.002 balanced-accuracy points on PSYCHE-D multiclass prediction, and remained close to the strongest references on PHQ-9 category and PSYCHE-D binary prediction. Ablations support Feature-wise Linear Modulation, absence tokens, missingness projections, and recursive refinement, while calibration and feature-source controls characterize endpoint behavior. Our code is available at https://github.com/Botwwt/MC-TRCM.

title: Tracing the Thoughts of a Coding Agent Playing ARC-AGI-3: Lessons for Continual Learning
abstract: We study how a coding agent learns across a sequence of abstract reasoning tasks. The agent runs on a frozen foundation model inside a fixed harness and acts by writing and running Python and shell scripts. It retains no state across turns other than its written artifacts, so every thought it forms, carries, corrects or abandons leaves a trace, where a thought is any belief, rule or plan committed to a file. We let the agent play ARC-AGI-3, a set of interactive reasoning games that provide no instructions. Each game is a sequence of levels, and a strategy that clears one level can fail on the next, so every new level is in effect a new task. The agent records what it learns as Python scripts and text notes, while the harness keeps a complete log of every action and observation. Our contribution is a measurement protocol that traces each thought through these files, from the task where it forms to the task where it is corrected or abandoned, applied to seven evaluation runs with three backbones from two model families. Scripts written for one task are almost never called again in a later task (33 of 630 references cross a task boundary), because most scripts embed the state of the current level. Instead, the agent rewrites its knowledge into new scripts, keeping the general rules and dropping the level-specific details, and abandons 74% of the scripts it wrote before a boundary. The notes, which only the model reads, are never revised: the agent appends without removing earlier claims, and the contradictions that accumulate are settled against the log. Because the log preserves everything, the agent forgets selectively, not catastrophically. The most costly error is a hard-coded value carried into a task where it no longer holds. These findings come from the files the agent wrote, without access to the model, and constitute a white-box analysis of how a coding agent continually learns.

title: Universal Construction and Exact Self-Reproduction in Ternary McCulloch-Pitts Networks
abstract: A fixed network of McCulloch-Pitts threshold units with weights in {-1,0,1} can hold other threshold networks in its state and run them: the state is a ring of banks of records, each record a unit of a stored network, and each step evaluates one record. We use such a network to carry out von Neumann's universal construction and self-reproduction exactly. As a cellular automaton keeps its rule, the fixed network keeps its weights, and what reproduces is a stored network. A constructor of 143 records reads the description of a network from its tape, builds that network in the next bank, copies the description onto the next tape and hands control to what it built; started on its own description, it rebuilds itself, weights included, in every generation. The scheme scales to a universal computer. A SUBLEQ computer of 17,598 ternary units, stored as 36,080 records and running a program of 27 instructions, builds any network that fits a bank and reproduces itself in the same way, at every word width from eight bits on; run directly, it emits the serialization of its own weights, memory and tape. Integer pre-activations give every orbit a margin of 1/2, and replicating each unit r times multiplies it by r. That suffices against noise of any size on the pre-activations, but against von Neumann's output flips only below a threshold inversely proportional to the fan-in. These results are proved in Rocq.

title: A 3D Characterization Framework for Intelligent Sequential Decision Making
abstract: Puzzles are widely used to evaluate the reasoning capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) systems for sequential decision making, yet approaches originating from different paradigms are rarely compared under unified conditions. To address this gap, we introduce a three-dimensional characterization framework that enables the analysts of AI methods by 1) projecting them to the Markov decision process (MDP) sequential decision making formalism, 2) degree of autonomy through human prior ranking of their designs and, 3) skill and computational cost. Using this framework, we analyze how representative graph-based, reinforcement learning, and large language model (LLM)-based approaches differ in their design choices and performance characteristics, instantiated respectively by Neurosolver, forward-backward reinforcement learning (FBRL), and automated thought-of-search (AutoToS), including a double-agent extension of thought-of-search (DA-ToS). The analysis relies on the Tower of Hanoi puzzle that provides a controlled benchmark with well-defined rules and scalable complexity, enabling consistent comparison across increasing problem sizes. The 3D characterization reveals that LLM-based methods, due to their weakly constrained action-space design, shift complexity from architecture to inference-time verification, leading to substantially higher memory and runtime costs than Neurosolver and FBRL.

title: Women Online Safety Index
abstract: The Women Online Safety Index (WOSI) is a dual-index analytical framework designed to measure platform-level safety for women by combining user-generated harm severity with platform moderation responsiveness. Unlike traditional comment-level toxicity detectors, WOSI evaluates entire platform ecosystems using empirical web scraping, natural language processing, fuzzy logic, and transparency data. The project includes the source code and analytical components used to calculate the indices and assess online platform safety. It aims to support systematic, data-driven evaluation of online harms and platform moderation practices affecting women.

title: Certified Scale Reuse and Embedded Boundary Responses in Recursive Networks — Reproducibility Archive
abstract: Reproducible scientific code, exact finite-network calculations, input specifications, raw outcomes and numerical evidence supporting the paper Certified Scale Reuse and Embedded Boundary Responses in Recursive Networks. The archive includes the original 192-geometry isolated boundary-response study (3,456 queries), a finite inner–outer extension with exact checks and a ten-assembly development pilot, and the separately prospectively specified E2 evaluation (30 base assemblies and six matched context companions). Certified correction, exact fallback, reference comparisons, neutral and adverse findings, raw timing and resource evidence, and reproducibility instructions are preserved. The earlier non-evaluable E1 attempt is documented separately and is neither a failed prediction nor an accepted result. The public E2 record has documented redactions of machine-local paths, without scientific model or matrix edits. Default reproduction checks saved data and selected representative workloads; it does not rerun the original complete timing campaigns.

title: SeDEx: a feature-map-aware semantic density explainer for CNN models
abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) use the hidden semantic meaning of the feature maps to make their decisions. Without considering the semantic meaning of the feature maps, we generally use untransparent metrics like F1-scores, precision, recall, and ROC curves to measure the quality of CNNs’ decisions. Hence, these metrics cannot facilitate explainability. Many explainability models such as SHAP, LIME and GradCAM can be found in artificial intelligence (AI) literature. However, they mainly focus on the connection between the decisions of the CNN models and the input features that develop explainability without integrating semantic meaning of the feature maps. Therefore, we need to develop feature-maps-aware explainability models to efficiently transform AI into explainable AI. We recently proposed an interpretable correlation map that extracts the semantic meaning of the feature maps and converts them into explainable correlation maps. However, correlation has several limitations, including (i) inability to prove causation and (ii) sensitivity to outliers that limit the bandwidth of explainability. This paper proposes a kernel density estimation (KDE) approach that can efficiently interpret the hidden semantic meaning of the feature maps and transform the feature maps into kernel density distributions, allowing bandwidth tuning to yield flexible and trustable explainability. In essence, it projects the semantic meaning of the feature maps of a pretrained CNN model into low-dimensional manifold using principal component analysis and models the joint density of semantic features using KDE. Hence, the predicted-class decomposition properties can be measured to determine the association between the KDE representations and the performance metrics. We have conducted an image classification experiment using a subset of the public dataset “102 Category Flower Dataset” and CNN-based VGG16, VGG19, and ResNet50 models. Experimental results show that there are connections between the high performance-scores and well-separated (and structured) density regions, and between the low performance-scores and the overlapping density regions

title: Chatbot service quality in omnichannel retailing: Effects of ChatbotSQ on decision confidence and customer behavior
abstract: AI chatbots are increasingly being embedded in omnichannel retail ecosystems; however, research on how chatbot service quality relates to customer behavior is limited. In this paper, we conceptualize chatbot service quality ( ChatbotSQ ) as a formative construct comprising six dimensions: functional, integration, interface, safety, emotional, and personalization quality. Drawing on means-end chain theory, we examine decision confidence as a mechanism underlying the association between chatbot service quality and customers' share of time with the chatbot and omnichannel ecosystem lock-in and explore the moderating role of chatbot comfort level. We use partial least squares structural equation modeling, importance-performance map analysis, and necessary condition analysis to analyze survey data from the United States ( N = 345) and Saudi Arabia ( N = 302). The results show that chatbot service quality is positively associated with customers' share of time with the chatbot and omnichannel ecosystem lock-in in both countries. These relationships are mediated by decision confidence, which also emerged as a necessary condition for achieving both behavioral outcomes. Chatbot comfort level significantly moderates the relationship between ChatbotSQ and decision confidence in Saudi Arabia but not in the United States, indicating that this boundary condition is context-sensitive across the two samples examined. We also validate a condensed six-item ChatbotSQ measure that provides a parsimonious alternative for research and practice. These findings advance retailing research by showing that AI chatbot service quality is associated with behavioral outcomes through customers’ decision confidence.

evidence.title: Chatbot service quality in omnichannel retailing: Effects of ChatbotSQ on decision confidence and customer behavior
evidence.abstract: AI chatbots are increasingly being embedded in omnichannel retail ecosystems; however, research on how chatbot service quality relates to customer behavior is limited. In this paper, we conceptualize chatbot service quality ( ChatbotSQ ) as a formative construct comprising six dimensions: functional, integration, interface, safety, emotional, and personalization quality. Drawing on means-end chain theory, we examine decision confidence as a mechanism underlying the association between chatbot service quality and customers' share of time with the chatbot and omnichannel ecosystem lock-in and explore the moderating role of chatbot comfort level. We use partial least squares structural equation modeling, importance-performance map analysis, and necessary condition analysis to analyze survey data from the United States ( N = 345) and Saudi Arabia ( N = 302). The results show that chatbot service quality is positively associated with customers' share of time with the chatbot and omnichannel ecosystem lock-in in both countries. These relationships are mediated by decision confidence, which also emerged as a necessary condition for achieving both behavioral outcomes. Chatbot comfort level significantly moderates the relationship between ChatbotSQ and decision confidence in Saudi Arabia but not in the United States, indicating that this boundary condition is context-sensitive across the two samples examined. We also validate a condensed six-item ChatbotSQ measure that provides a parsimonious alternative for research and practice. These findings advance retailing research by showing that AI chatbot service quality is associated with behavioral outcomes through customers’ decision confidence.

title: LLM Hallucination of Citations in Economics Persists With Web‐Enabled Models
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite significant advances since 2023 in large language model (LLM) capabilities and the introduction of web‐enabled search functionality, citation hallucination remains a persistent problem in AI‐generated academic content. We test GPT‐4o, DeepSeek V3, web‐enabled GPT‐4o, and web‐enabled GPT‐5.1 across prompts derived from Journal of Economic Literature categories. Using a hierarchical citation validation framework, we find that even an advanced web‐enabled model produces non‐existent citations. While web‐enabled models show improvement over their predecessors, the error rates remain high for scholarly applications. Our findings suggest that the fundamental challenge of citation hallucination persists despite technological advances, with implications for academic integrity and the reliable use of AI in research contexts. We provide an online tool for researchers to run LLMs through the benchmark test using our prompts.

title: Behind-the-Meter Photovoltaic Visibility from Net Smart Meters: Deployment Regimes and Operational Insights
abstract: Distribution operators need visibility of behind-the-meter photovoltaic (PV) generation, yet most residential customers are observed only through net smart meters. Deep-learning-based PV disaggregation can restore this visibility, but its operational value depends on whether the model serves known customers, new customers, future periods, or new regions. We quantify this dependence using four deployment regimes that separate household transfer from temporal extrapolation, applied to Ausgrid smart-meter data with cross-dataset adaptation to the Pecan Street data. Using a fixed training protocol, we benchmark representative deep sequence architectures for PV disaggregation under regime-matched evaluation. At a fixed 48-hour context length, daylight mean absolute error (MAE) of the best model rises from 0.104~kW on seen households in the future test period to 0.185~kW on unseen households over the same period, and under a fixed training contract the deployment regime explains far more of the error variation than model choice. Under target-domain normalization, fine-tuning on five target-region households reduces source-model transfer error by 28\%--36\%. Long input windows help known-customer extrapolation, while their new-customer benefits vary by model. These findings suggest regime-matched error budgets, limited target supervision for model adaptation in new regions, and use-case-dependent context selection for energy data analytics.

title: High-Dimensional Two-Sample Covariance Testing with Null-Preserving Transformations
abstract: Testing equality of two high-dimensional covariance matrices is challenging when many entries differ only slightly. Dependence among sample covariance entries can also affect the finite-sample size and power of tests that aggregate their differences. We propose a studentized ell_2-type statistic that averages squared, marginally standardized differences between corresponding entries of the two sample covariance matrices. Before constructing the statistic, we apply the same nonsingular linear transformation to both samples. In the transformed coordinates, the covariance-equality hypothesis is unchanged, whereas the standardized differences and correlations among their estimators generally change. The transformation can therefore incorporate structural or scientific information without reducing dimension. We approximate the null distribution using a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap that uses coordinatewise studentization and avoids forming or inverting the full covariance matrix of the vectorized sample covariance entries. For deterministic transformations, we derive nonasymptotic Gaussian and bootstrap approximation bounds and establish asymptotic size validity and power consistency. We also show that replacing a population transformation by a same-sample estimator leaves the statistic and bootstrap critical value asymptotically unchanged in relative terms under an operator-norm convergence condition. Simulations show that suitable transformations improve size accuracy and power under weak dependence. An analysis of breast cancer gene-expression data illustrates the method.

title: PageWeaver: KV-Guided Query Unions for Sparse Attention
abstract: Dynamic sparse attention limits the KV pages selected by each query, but a small support does not necessarily yield efficient GPU work. Query unions share page loads and populate Tensor Core tiles; their cost depends on which queries are grouped together. We present PageWeaver, an execution design that uses selected-page affinity to assemble query groups while preserving each query's original support and complete output ownership. A bounded GPU search produces query IDs, and an ID-aware two-CTA kernel consumes them without materializing reordered Q tensors or cross-page partial outputs. A direct KV-page union implementation provides a complementary design study of nonlocal reuse and reduction cost. With FP8 KV throughout, the H200 Union8 implementation achieves a 1.70x geometric-mean complete-call speedup over the measured FlashInfer path on six captures. Online regrouping further lowers latency by 3.26-7.66% on five selected 64K-context captures. Whole-model prefill throughput is 7.88-14.36% above the tested native path; the incremental regrouping benefit is smaller, with observed median gains of 0.47-0.73% at 32K/64K and regressions at 8K. A B300 comparison identifies cases where preparation cost and a stronger native kernel remove the advantage. These results separate execution-group reuse from the complete cost of exploiting it online.

title: Composable logical gate error in approximate quantum error correction: reexamining gate implementations in Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codes
abstract: Quantifying the accuracy of logical gates is paramount in approximate error correction, where perfect implementations are often unachievable with the available set of physical operations. To this end, we introduce a single scalar quantity we call the (composable) logical gate error. It captures both the deviation of the logical action from the desired target gate as well as leakage out of the code space. It is subadditive under successive application of gates, providing a simple means for analyzing circuits. We show how to bound the composable logical gate error in terms of matrix elements of physical unitaries between (approximate) logical computational basis states. In the continuous-variable context, this sidesteps the need for computing energy-bounded norms. As an example, we study the composable logical gate error for linear optics implementations of Paulis and Cliffords in approximate Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes. We find that the logical gate error for implementations of Paulis depends linearly on the squeezing parameter. This implies that their accuracy improves monotonically with the amount of squeezing. For some Cliffords, however, linear optics implementations which are exact for ideal GKP codes fail in the approximate case: they have a constant logical gate error even in the limit of infinite squeezing. This is consistent with previous results about the limitations of certain gate implementations for approximate GKP codes. It shows that findings applicable to ideal GKP codes do not always translate to the realm of physically realizable approximate GKP codes.

title: Efficient quadratic entropy with distance sketches
abstract: We detail scalable methods for approximating the quadratic entropy $p^T d p$ for arbitrary distributions $p$ and common distances $d$ of negative type. We focus on the Euclidean and spherical geodesic cases, which both use random feature embeddings and projections to dramatically improve computational complexity within a simple framework. Amortization of a single large matrix multiplication and control variates further enable computation at large scale with low memory and runtime in situations where $d$ is held constant while $p$ varies. We demonstrate this with a comparison against direct pair sampling and bibliometric/scientometric examples on Open Graph Benchmark datasets, revealing papers, fields, and institutions with both particularly narrow and broad interdisciplinary reach from their citations and text features alone.

title: Quantum correlation preserving frequency conversion in pressurized hydrogen
abstract: Quantum computers are expected to offer significant advantages over classical computers by using quantum mechanical phenomena such as superposition and entanglement. Potential future quantum networks may rely on hybrid architectures that combine the advantages of different qubit platforms. In such networks, quantum information must be transferred between stationary and flying qubits, typically photons. A major challenge, however, is that different quantum systems operate at vastly different wavelengths, making direct interconnection impossible. This challenge is addressed by quantum frequency conversion (QFC), which enables the transfer of quantum information between different spectral regions while preserving the quantum state. Most current QFC approaches employ the second-order nonlinearity of crystals. An alternative approach is based on the third-order nonlinearity of gases. In particular, coherent Raman scattering processes such as coherent Stokes and anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CSRS/CARS) enable polarization-independent, broadband and tunable frequency conversion through virtual energy levels. Within the Cluster of Excellence Matter and Light for Quantum Computing (ML4Q), a hydrogen-filled hollow-core fiber is used to realize continuous-wave CSRS-based frequency conversion. The goal is to convert photons emitted by InAs/GaAs quantum dots at approximately 865 nm into the telecom O-band around 1350 nm, thereby enabling the use of these quantum dots in fiber-based quantum communication networks. In this thesis, the conversion stage evolved from a short gas-cell configuration to a hollow-core fiber system providing interaction lengths of several meters. The development and optimization of the experimental setup, including the selection of laser wavelengths, hollow-core fibers, and the design of custom hydrogen chambers are discussed. A detailed characterization of the frequency-conversion system is performed, focusing on the dependence of the conversion efficiency on pressure, intensity, and interaction length, as well as on polarization and bandwidth. Special attention is given to conversion efficiency compared to optical losses and background contributions, which ultimately limit the performance of the current implementation. The key challenges are identified and potential strategies for future improvements are discussed. The central achievement of this work is the experimental demonstration of quantum-correlation-preserving frequency conversion. Using entangled photon pairs generated by spontaneous parametric down-conversion, the preservation of quantum correlations is verified by comparing the cross-correlation functions before and after the conversion process. This work lays the foundation for further experiments with continuous-wave CSRS-based quantum frequency conversion, including measurements with InAs/GaAs quantum dots.

title: Auditing Trajectory-Based Transfer Diagnostics in Variational Quantum Learning
abstract: Trajectory-derived scalars are often used to assess few-shot adaptation in variational quantum learning, but their associations may reflect optimization geometry rather than out-of-sample transfer. We audit parameter drift, an observable-variance proxy, and support–query gradient alignment in Heisenberg/XYZ tasks with 4–10 qubits and circuit depths 2, 3, and 5. A one-step expansion links alignment to validation improvement; the alignment–improvement rank correlation rises from 0.60 to 0.85 as gradient magnitudes and adaptation steps shrink, and the alignment–gap association is near zero for each pooled size after adjustment for improvement and initial query loss, with heterogeneous configuration effects. Target decomposition shows that this adjusted null does not establish absence of transfer information. Four controls bound the interpretation: under an independent support–validation–test split, validation-set alignment has no rank association with improvement on unseen observables (ρ≈0 at n=6,8), also in a family with positive transfer; with a fixed Pauli-term count the shrinkage of the mean gradient norm largely disappears while the identity strengthening persists; depolarizing noise strengthens the identity link; and the ansatz is near-Haar expressible throughout. Drift tracks support improvement, and the variance proxy remains near zero. These results motivate an audit checklist for trajectory scalars.

title: Advancing LLM-based 5G traffic classification: a multi-layer evaluation of performance and reasoning reliability
abstract: Abstract The rapid proliferation of 5G networks has enabled a wide range of data-intensive applications, including video streaming, online gaming, metaverse platforms, and real-time communication services. Understanding the behavior and characteristics of such heterogeneous traffic is essential for efficient network management, resource allocation, and quality of service (QoS) optimization. However, most existing studies rely on simulated or synthetic datasets, limiting their applicability to real-world scenarios. This paper presents a comprehensive data-driven analysis of 5G traffic using a large-scale real-world dataset collected from commercial mobile networks. The dataset consists of over 328 h of traffic captured from diverse applications, including Netflix, YouTube Live, Zoom, Roblox, and cloud gaming platforms, using mobile-based packet capture tools without specialized hardware. The collected data is processed into a time-series format with packet-level features, enabling detailed traffic characterization and analysis. We investigate the effectiveness of machine learning and large language models (LLMs) in classifying and analyzing 5G traffic patterns across multiple application categories. Experimental results reveal that traditional structured machine learning approaches outperform LLM-based models in handling network traffic classification tasks, particularly in multi-class and imbalanced scenarios. Furthermore, LLM-based methods exhibit high rates of inconsistency and prediction bias, highlighting their limitations when applied to structured network data. The findings of this study provide practical insights into the suitability of different AI approaches for real-world 5G traffic analysis. The proposed framework contributes to the development of more reliable and efficient traffic classification systems, supporting advanced network optimization, intelligent traffic management, and future 5G/6G deployments.

title: Agentic Software Porting: Lessons from the CHERI-PIT
abstract: Porting C/C++ software to new hardware is an agent-shaped problem. The source changes stay small, but each one requires scarce expert diagnosis of compiler warnings and hardware faults. This experience paper reports eight lessons from six months of developing CHERI-PIT, a system still under active development. CHERI-PIT is an LLM-agent pipeline that ports C/C++ projects to the memory-safe pure-capability (purecap) ABI of CHERI hardware on Arm Morello. The pipeline has carried 29 upstream projects to reproducible port recipes. Verifier scripts measured zero CHERI faults over each ported project’s test baselines on Morello hardware. The corpus includes a working PostgreSQL server and a complete CRuby interpreter. The lessons fall into three themes: dividing the labor so one pipeline survives project scale, verifying progress mechanically so no claim of success rests on the agent’s own report, and retaining insight gained through porting so the tool grows more capable with each port. Each lesson unfolds as an evolution: what CHERI-PIT initially did, what we observed, and what we changed The lessons together trace a path toward a porting tool that emits reproducible and auditable port recipes.

title: Semantic Views: Certified Reuse of LLM Labels Across Semantic Queries
abstract: Semantic query engines evaluate natural-language filters with a large language model, and every evaluation is a costly oracle call. Optimizers that reduce these calls face a dilemma: cascades that trust a cheap proxy miss their precision and recall targets on many queries, methods with finite-sample guarantees save little, and all of them discard the oracle's labels when the query ends. We present SemViews, a certified semantic filter that orders tuples by signals that cost no oracle calls (the labels that earlier queries left behind as semantic views, a local embedding, and a helper model's score), refines that order with labels it must pay for anyway, and certifies its answer with fresh stratified oracle samples. The answer meets user precision and recall targets with probability at least $1-δ$ for every workload and every catalog, so a stale or misleading view can cost oracle calls but never accuracy. On four workloads replayed against 725,000 recorded oracle labels, SemViews meets both targets on 99.63% of queries and saves 28%-45% of the oracle calls, whereas the only prior method in our study with the same guarantee needs 1.32x-1.71x as many calls. When a question returns in different words, views cut its calls by a further 27%-36%, with both targets met on at least 99.8% of such queries; similarity caches and entailment-based reuse meet them on only 17%-47%.
